label: Stable Maps
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 115 through 152 and asks why a sequence of J-holomorphic spheres compactifies to a decorated tree of spheres rather than a single map. Bubbling forces us to remember domain degeneration, and Kontsevich's stable maps package that memory into a compact moduli space.

label: Why Single Maps Fail
notes: Energy concentrating at a point makes derivatives blow up, so the naive limit loses a piece of the curve. We rescale near the concentration point to recover the lost energy as a bubble sphere attached at a node, motivating a domain that is a tree, not one sphere.

label: Nodal Domains as Trees
notes: The prestable domain is a finite tree of spheres glued at nodal points, one shared pair per edge. Marked points sit on vertices. The dual graph records incidence, and because the graph is a tree the genus stays zero throughout the bubbling process described in this chapter.

label: The Stable Map
notes: A stable map is a J-holomorphic map from a nodal curve whose components fit together continuously at nodes. The map carries energy on each component, and the total energy is the symplectic area of the homology class, conserved across every degeneration limit we study here.

label: The Stability Condition
notes: Stability demands finitely many automorphisms. A nonconstant component is rigid through its image, but a ghost component is constant and only special points pin its Mobius group. The rule requires every constant component to carry at least three special points, nodes plus marks combined.

label: Ghost Components
notes: A ghost component carries zero energy yet is structurally necessary. It may appear when a marked point collides with another mark or lands on a node during bubbling. Stability forces it to have three special points, otherwise it would retain residual Mobius freedom and break compactness of the space.

label: The Equivalence Relation
notes: Two stable maps are equivalent when a tree isomorphism plus one Mobius reparametrization per component identifies them. Component labels may change, but incidence, energy, nodal positions, and marked values must remain compatible. Quotienting by this relation kills the infinitesimal automorphisms stability already bounded.

label: Gromov Convergence
notes: Gromov convergence is a coordinated limit, not pointwise convergence on one sphere. Maps converge smoothly on compact sets away from nodes, rescalings match the two sides of each shrinking neck, and the energy axiom forces every bubble's energy to reappear exactly at its node.

label: Rescaling and Bubbling
notes: Near a bubbling point we apply Mobius rescalings with parameter tending to zero. The parent chart sees a shrinking disc while the bubble chart magnifies it into a full sphere. The collapsing neck annulus becomes a node, and opposite source points match across the new edge.

label: Compactness
notes: Bubble extraction grows a finite weighted tree by zooming at unresolved concentration points. It terminates because every nonconstant bubble carries energy above a positive threshold while the total energy is bounded. The resulting tree is stable, giving subsequential Gromov limits for any bounded sequence.

label: Uniqueness and Topology
notes: Uniqueness compares two systems of rescalings and rules out an unaccounted intermediate bubble, recovering the tree isomorphism. Rho-style neighborhoods then translate Gromov convergence into a first-countable Hausdorff topology, so two candidate limits of one sequence must define equivalent decorated trees.

label: Compact and Hausdorff
notes: The space of stable maps is compact, Hausdorff, and metrizable. Compactness supplies limits, uniqueness makes them well defined up to equivalence, and continuity of the evaluation and forgetful maps lets the moduli space support the intersection theory built in later chapters of the book.
